terms.grammar: tempus est with an infinitive; the person, if named, as subject accusative or dative
evidence: Liv. 21.54.2: nunc corpora cūrāre tempus est
Cic. Top. 1.5: sed jam tempus est ad id quod īnstituimus accēdere (Lewis & Short s.v. tempus)
terms.comment: English “it’s time to” goes word for word: tempus est surgere, it’s time to get up. With a person: tempus est mē abīre (Cic. Tusc. 1.99) or tibi abīre (Hor. Epist. 2.2.215).

terms.grammar: tempus est with the genitive of a noun or gerund
evidence: Sen. Ep. 122.9: lūcet: somnī tempus est
terms.comment: “Time for sleep”, “time for supper”: the thing in the genitive.

phrases.english: now it is time to look after ourselves (food, a bath, rest)
it’s getting light: time for bed!

sources: Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-livius, loci-seneca-epistulae), checked against the editions named there.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 35, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
